messages.subject: map_data ()
parts:
Hi,

I am most impressed how easy it now is to draw simple choropleth maps
using the new function map_data (), as detailed in the new version of
Hadley's book. However, I am at a loss as to how to get map_data () to
use map objects created from shape files, or objects such as
'wrld_simpl' in package maptools. The world data that comes with the
library maps is quite outdated, with Russian Federation still named
USSR and many countries missing.

Here is the code I am using:

> nword <- read.shape ('general_2008') # refers to files with extensions .shp, .prj, .shx, .dbf

> class (nworld)
[1] "Map"

> plot (nworld) # works fine: this draws a map of the world

Such map objects are not what map_data likes and I have no idea how to
convert the nworld object.

I also tried:

> nworld.poly <- readShapePoly ('general_2008')

> class (nworld.poly)
[1] "polylist"

> plot (nworld.poly) # also works

The same goes with wrld_simpl in maptools:

> library (maptools)
> data (wrld_simpl)
> plot (wrld_simpl) # works

> map_data ('wrld_simpl')
Error in get(dbname) : variable "wrld_simplMapEnv" was not found
In addition: Warning message:
In data(list = dbname) : data set 'wrld_simplMapEnv' not found


Any help would be appreciated,

Philippe

messages.subject: Re: map_data ()
parts:
Dear Hadley,

I attached high-def shape files that I use almost every day. R reads
them fine with maptools::readShapeSpatial (), which creates an object
of class SpatialPolygonsDataFrame (sp). I pasted below my signature
the code that I use to create choropleth maps (after adding the
variable inc_all to the main dbf data file). I would definitely prefer
to use ggplot for this, as ggplot2 graphs look so much nicer and your
map_data () function does a very elegant job at converting something
obscure (to me) into something very clear to understand. I do not
understand how sp objects are structured (I just know how to access
the embedded dataframe where there is one). Thanks a lot for offering
your help again. I hope the compressed attachment is not too big.

Best wishes,

Philippe



###
library (maptools)
library (RColorBrewer)
library (classInt)

setwd ('D:/glaziou/data/2009/maps')

# read high-density shape files
who3 <- readShapeSpatial ('who')

# read legal stuff with disputed borders
maskline <- readShapeSpatial ('maskline08_general')
maskpoly <- readShapeSpatial ('maskpoly08_general')

# extract data of interest
plotvar <- who3@data$inc_all

# prepare breaks and colours
nclr <- 6
plotclr <- brewer.pal (nclr, 'BuPu')
class <- classIntervals(plotvar, nclr, style="fixed",
fixedBreaks=c(0,20,50,100,200,500,1200))
colcode <- findColours (class, plotclr)

# plot map and legend
plot (who3, col=colcode)
legend(-170, -25, legend=names(attr(colcode, "table")),
fill=attr(colcode, "palette"), cex=0.6, bty="n")

# add disputed borders to the plot
plot (maskline, add=T)
plot (maskpoly, add=T)

messages.author: b756a7daa2c2aa6d
messages.subject: Re: map_data ()
parts:
Hi Phillippe,

Below, I've included some code I've used previously for turning shape
files into data frames. It doesn't work with the lines, but does with
your other two shapefiles. (It should also work for cases where each
main region is composed of multiple polygons, if you adapt the line
beginning with polys <-). The main problem is for such large datasets
you really need to be able thin (aka generalise) the map boundaries
and there isn't any code in R to do so, and so far my attempts to
write a topologically consistent polyline simplification algorithm
have not been successful.

Hadley

library(plyr)
library(gpclib)

invert <- function (L) {
t1 <- unlist(L)
names(t1) <- rep(names(L), lapply(L, length))
tapply(names(t1), t1, c)
}

get_attributes <- function(shape) {
attr <- as.data.frame(shape)
names(attr) <- tolower(names(attr))

attr
}

get_borders <- function(shape) {
attr <- get_attributes(shape)
cp <- polygons(shape)

# Figure out how polygons should be split up into the region of interest
# Currently just assume that this given by the first variable in the
# attributes
polys <- split(as.numeric(row.names(attr)), list(attr[, 1]))

# Union together all polygons that make up a region
unioned <- unionSpatialPolygons(cp, invert(polys))

# Extract coordinates of regions
get_coords <- function(x) {
df <- as.data.frame(x@polygons[[1]]@Polygons[[1]]@coords)
names(df) <- c("long", "lat")
df
}
coords <- llply(seq_along(polys), function(i) get_coords(unioned[i]))

thinned <- coords

# Add column to identify region
named <- mlply(cbind(df = thinned, id = names(polys)),
function(df, id) transform(df, id = id))

do.call("rbind", named)
}


Hadley
